issues.legal_issue: A statute authorizing acquisition of any land or rights in land applies to land and rights owned by a State when its text does not exclude State property.
material_facts: The statute authorized acquisition of “any land” or “any rights in or over such land” without restricting those terms by reference to the owner.

A proviso required prior consultation with a State government before acquisition of its unleased land or rights, and other provisions addressed situations in which the acquiring government became lessee of a State government.
The State argued that the statute was intended to acquire only private interests and did not apply to land it owned.
issues.conclusion: The statute, properly construed, applies to land and rights owned by a State; the State’s challenge to its application was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The statute’s operative language governs its scope. A statement of objects and reasons cannot be used to cut down the generality of the enacted text, and the preamble did not exclude State property. The proviso requiring consultation with the State government supported the conclusion that State-owned land was within the operative provisions.

predicates.challenge_to_statutory_scope: A litigant challenged whether a statute authorizing acquisition applies to property owned by a State.
predicates.statute_uses_unqualified_land_terms: The statute describes the property subject to acquisition in general terms without limiting those terms by the identity of its owner.
predicates.statute_provides_for_consultation_with_s: The statute requires consultation with a State government before a specified acquisition of land or rights belonging to it.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns the scope of an acquisition statute, unqualified land terms together with a consultation provision for State-owned property result in the statute applying to that property.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional allocation of powers does not make the States absolutely sovereign or immune from valid Union legislation affecting their property.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether Union legislation could reach property owned by a State.
The Constitution distributes legislative and executive powers between the Union and the States, with significant powers assigned to the Union.
The Constitution permits Parliament to alter State boundaries and even to extinguish a State by law.
The State relied on its asserted sovereignty to argue that its property was beyond Union legislative power.
issues.conclusion: The States do not possess full or absolute sovereignty that prevents Parliament from legislating in a manner affecting State property.
issues.legal_principle: The majority considered the constitutional allocation of powers, including Articles 73, 162, 246, 248 and 249, and the Union’s authority to alter State boundaries under Articles 2 and 3. It concluded that the Constitution is not truly federal in character in the sense asserted and that the distribution of powers does not give States absolute sovereignty. The judgment discussed McCulloch v. Maryland, Bank of Toronto v. Lambe and Webb v. Outrim in considering limits on legislative power and rejected immunity based merely on the possibility that a power might be abused.

predicates.constitutional_allocation_dispute: A proceeding disputes whether the constitutional relationship between national and regional governments limits national authority.
predicates.union_and_states_have_distributed_powers: The constitution assigns legislative and executive powers to both the national government and regional governments.
predicates.parliament_can_alter_state_boundaries: The constitution authorizes the national legislature to change the territories or boundaries of regional governments.

issues.definition: Where a constitutional allocation dispute arises under a system that distributes powers but allows the national legislature to alter regional boundaries, the regional governments are not absolutely sovereign.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament has legislative competence to authorize acquisition of property owned by a State under its acquisition power, including when the acquisition supports national regulation of an industry or resource.
material_facts: Parliament enacted legislation authorizing acquisition of coal-bearing land and rights for development of the coal industry.
The legislation pursued greater public control over coal mining and mineral development under national control.

The Constitution assigned acquisition and requisition of property to a concurrent legislative field and assigned Parliament powers concerning industries and the regulation of mines and mineral development under Union control.
The State contended that Parliament could not use its acquisition power to acquire State property.
issues.conclusion: Parliament is competent to enact a law providing for acquisition of State property; the challenged statute was not ultra vires on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 42 of List III, read with Article 246, empowers Parliament to legislate concerning acquisition and requisition of property. That power is not restricted to privately owned property and may support the exercise of powers under Entries 52 and 54 of List I concerning industries and mines under Union control. Articles 294 and 298 do not bar acquisition of State property. The majority relied on the broad construction of legislative powers and discussed United States v. Darby, State of Oklahoma ex rel. Phillips v. Guy F. Atkinson Company, Kohl v. United States, Attorney-General for British Columbia v. Canadian Pacific Railway Company and Attorney-General for Quebec v. Nipissing Central Railway Company.

predicates.challenge_to_parliamentary_acquisition_p: A proceeding challenges Parliament’s authority to legislate for compulsory acquisition of property owned by a State.
predicates.constitution_assigns_concurrent_acquisit: The constitution assigns legislative authority over acquisition of property to both national and regional legislatures.
predicates.national_legislation_pursues_control_of_: The national legislature has enacted a law to advance national control or regulation of an industry or resource.
predicates.target_property_is_state_owned: The property that the national law authorizes the government to acquire is owned by a regional government.

issues.definition: When Parliament’s acquisition power is challenged, a concurrent constitutional grant, national legislation pursuing control of an industry or resource, and State-owned target property permit Parliament to legislate for that acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: State-owned property is protected by the constitutional requirements governing compulsory acquisition, including a public purpose and provision for compensation.
material_facts: The statute authorized compulsory acquisition of land and rights, including interests owned by a State.
The State disputed Parliament’s authority to acquire its property, and the Court considered whether constitutional protections for acquisition applied to State property.
issues.conclusion: State property may not be acquired under an acquisition law unless that law complies with the applicable requirements of Article 31.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2) protects property against compulsory acquisition except for a public purpose and under a law providing for compensation in the constitutionally specified manner. The majority read Article 31(2) together with Entry 42 of List III, treating the term “property” as including State property. It relied on Kavalappara Kottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras and discussed Article 13 and Director of Rationing and Distribution v. Corporation of Calcutta in addressing constitutional protections and the interpretation of general legal language.

predicates.challenge_to_compulsory_acquisition_law: A proceeding challenges a law that authorizes compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.law_authorizes_compulsory_acquisition: The challenged law provides for the compulsory taking of property by government.
predicates.target_property_is_state_owned: The property subject to the proposed taking is owned by a regional government.

issues.definition: When a compulsory-acquisition law is challenged and its target property belongs to a regional government, that property is protected by the applicable acquisition requirements.
